runs.text: Pareas das molheres que parem: mas a pro

lines.note: Iya denotes the afterbirth, as shown by the reference to women giving birth. The gloss contrasts it with the more proper term Yena below; pro continues into pria without a printed terminal hyphen.
Completes propria palaura: the dictionary prefers Yena, corresponding to ena, as the name for the afterbirth. Yena is a Japanese word embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Iyagaki is writing the same thing twice. The Portuguese infinitive escreuer establishes the repeated-writing sense rather than an interpretation based on the modern negative iya.
Iyagaki suru adds the verb suru to the preceding noun; Idem explicitly repeats the same act of writing twice.
Iyagari, iyagaru, iyagatta expresses unwillingness or resistance. The principal parts agree with the Portuguese alternatives of not wanting and finding something repugnant.
Iy ai introduces reciprocal speaking, with historical long-vowel principal parts. Docoye begins the example asking where someone went; the first letter is capital I, not the OCR lowercase l.
Gocǒ naſaretacato iy auaruru continues the respectful question and the reciprocal saying. Feiq. is the citation label; the italic Lib. leads into its book number on the next row.

runs.text: 3. Falarão entre ſi perguntando hum ao outro

lines.note: Book 3 concludes the citation. The translation describes people speaking among themselves and asking one another; the scan shows a stop after the numeral.
Onde hia completes the indirect question, asking where the person was going. Historical hia is retained rather than modernized to ia.
Iyaitoco denotes second cousins. The following clause introduces Futaitoco as another name; the scan supports Tambem rather than the OCR Tanbem.
Futaitoco is the alternative word for second cousins introduced by Tambem se diz above. Its indentation reflects continuation of that entry.
This first Iya iya entry is the negative expression, translated literally as no, no. Adu. is the italic grammatical label.

runs.text: Interieição do que louua, ouen care-

lines.note: The repeated headword now introduces an admiring interjection used in praising or extolling something. The printed separation ouen care- is retained rather than silently respaced to modern ou encarece.
Completes encarecer something and begins the admiring example, Iya iya migotona koto. The scan shows a word space before migotona, which was absent from the OCR.

runs.text: O couſa apraziuel, ou pera ver.

lines.note: To completes koto. The Portuguese exclamation describes something pleasing or worth seeing, confirming that this Iya iya expresses admiration rather than refusal.

Iyamaxi and iyamaxini express increasing degree; the Japanese paraphrase begins Iyoiyo and continues below. The alternative marker l and the adverb label are apparatus, not part of the Japanese words.
Maſu completes iyoiyo masu, increasing more and more. The Portuguese crecendo is retained as printed instead of being regularized to crescendo.
Iya mezzuraxij is explained by Icanimo mezzuraxij, something exceptionally novel or remarkable. Cou begins the Portuguese noun continued below, without a visible terminal hyphen.
Completes the gloss as very new and pleasing. S. is the upright written-usage label, not part of the italic Portuguese sentence.
Iyana and iyano qualify something unwanted or displeasing. The relative clause continues below and leads to an example of an unwelcome thing.
Completes the sense of something that does not please the speaker. Iyana cotogia means that it is an unwelcome or disagreeable thing, with historical gia for the copula.
Iyanaxǔ, alternatively iyana fito, denotes an objectionable person. The Portuguese peſſoa confirms a person rather than an abstract quality; the printed vowel mark is retained.

runs.text: & com que não folgo de tratar.

lines.note: Completes the personal description: someone whose company or dealings the speaker does not enjoy. This belongs to Iyanaxǔ, not the following speaking verb.
Iy arauaſu means expressing or declaring something in words. The printed space between Iy and arauaſu is preserved despite their compound interpretation.
Iy ate, with the historical tçuru form, means hitting on the correct answer or guessing correctly in speech. The printed Portuguese a deuinhar separation is retained.
De palaura specifies verbal guessing or stating the right answer and completes the gloss above. The short row is a genuine continuation.
Iy auaxe means consulting or discussing something with another person. The principal form ſuru belongs to the historical inflection of awase, not a separate modern suru construction.

runs.text: tro ſobre algum negocio, ou aſſentar com elle

lines.note: Completes outro and explains discussing a matter or reaching an arrangement with the other person. The object of aſſentar continues below.
Algũa couſa completes the agreement or settlement described in the preceding row. The tilde remains over the printed u.

Iyaxi, iyaſu, with the printed past ending aita, denotes healing. The example begins wound or illness, with ya- continuing below. The visible initial I was omitted by OCR; the historical aita is not modernized.
Maiuo completes yamaiuo, illness as an object of iyaſu; qizu supplies the alternative wound. The Portuguese describes curing a wound or disease, so iyaſu is transitive here.
Ou doença completes the second object of curing, parallel to ferida above. It remains a separate physical continuation line.
Iyaxij means base, low, or contemptible. This is the adjective iyashii, distinct from the preceding healing verb despite the shared initial letters.
Iyaxiſa is the corresponding noun for baseness or lowliness. The scan supports a continuous word rather than the OCR space in Iya xiſa.
Iyaxǔ is the adverbial form of the preceding adjective. The initial is capital I, not long s; the historical marked-u ending is preserved.
Iyaxime, iyaximuru, iyaximeta means despising or treating as contemptible. The Portuguese deſprezar distinguishes it from merely becoming low.

runs.text: Hũa caixa de figura ouada em que

lines.note: Iybitçu names an oval box used for cooked rice. The Japanese initial I and the rice-container context correct OCR lybitçu; ouada describes its egg-like shape.
The box holds cooked rice. Iybitçu nari introduces its oval form or shape; it is an independent Japanese illustrative phrase, not a word inserted syntactically into the Portuguese gloss.
Gura completes Fi-gura, followed by a second Portuguese word for shape. The printed desta is retained without a global st/ſt normalization.
Iycaqe means putting an accusation or matter to someone, with further senses developed below. The capital I replaces the OCR l; the Portuguese here introduces the imputing sense.
The cited example begins with Yoritomo hearing something and being presented with a nandai, a difficult or unreasonable demand. The verb iy caqeraruru continues across the row boundary.
Completes the interrogative verb and identifies the Feiq. citation. The Portuguese repeats the name Yoritomo; its first letter is Y, not the OCR V, and the name is embedded in the italic explanation.

runs.text: diße impondes me couſas ſem razão, & de

lines.note: The translation reports Yoritomo objecting that unreasonable and troublesome things are being imposed on him. Printed diße retains the supplied historical ligature representation.

runs.text: embaraço? ¶ Item, Propor a alguem algũa

lines.note: Embaraço completes the question about troublesome demands; the scan has a question mark, not a full stop. A new sense then introduces proposing a matter to someone.
Completes the sense of opening a conversation by putting a matter forward. Fuxinuo iy begins the example of presenting a doubt or question.
Caquru completes the example, explicitly translated as proposing a doubt. The next Item starts a third sense: having begun to speak without finishing.

runs.text: começado de falar, & não acabado algũa cou

lines.note: Continues the unfinished-speaking sense. The final cou continues as ſa at the top of column 2; the scan does not establish a terminal hyphen, so none is supplied.
The opening ſa completes couſa from column 1. Iy caqete voita cotouo tanomi begins a request concerning something the speaker had started to say.

runs.text: O que comecei a falar encomendo

lines.note: Zonzuru completes the respectful request. The Portuguese begins entrusting or recommending the matter previously raised to the addressee.
Volo completes the preceding encomendo construction, followed by an emphatic request. The historical pronoun sequence and spacing are retained as printed.

Iycachi, iycatçu, iycatta means winning or prevailing through words. An ink blot obscures much of the initial I; the surviving word and bilingual sense support Iycachi rather than OCR bycachi, with that initial remaining a nonblocking damaged-glyph caveat. The subsequently consulted NINJAL Entry Words Data (version 202510; Hideyuki Ohshima, assisted by Taichi Aida; CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html) independently supports this lexical identification, not the exact typography.
Iycaſume means concealing or obscuring something by words. The gloss continues into the explanation of verbal excuses on the next row.

runs.text: palauras eſcuſandoſe do que lhe impoem, &c.

lines.note: The concealment consists in excusing oneself against something imputed to one. The Portuguese eſcuſandoſe provides the link between concealment and verbal self-defence.
Togauo iycaſumuru illustrates verbally concealing or excusing a fault. The final eſcu continues below without a visible line-end hyphen.
The opening ſar completes eſcuſar. The Portuguese makes the object sins or faults excused through words; it belongs to the example, not another entry.
Iycatame means confirming or making something firm by speech. The gloss does not introduce a physical hardening sense here.
Iycauaxi denotes exchanging words or conversing with one another. Com- begins the Portuguese alternative communicarſe across the physical line break.
Municarſe completes communicarſe, here communicating in conversation. This is the second Portuguese paraphrase of exchanging words.
Iycaxiqi is explained by Mexiuo coxirayuru, preparing rice. This is a rice-related iy- word, not another compound of speaking merely because it occurs among such entries.
Completes aparelhar and adds cozer arroz, cooking rice. The Portuguese confirms the food-preparation interpretation of the preceding Japanese forms.
Iychiguiri means establishing friendship or an agreement by words. The principal parts fit a chigiru verb; the Portuguese word palauras is divided below.

runs.text: lauras, ou fazer concerto entre ſi.

lines.note: Completes the verbal-friendship explanation and adds making an agreement with one another. Concerto is retained in its historical agreement sense.
Iychiraxi means spreading a report or making something widely known. The scan supports the historical diuulgar with two u letters, rather than the OCR diulgar.
Iycutaxi means speaking disparagingly or belittling someone. The printed Deſdanhar and desfazer are preserved without modernizing the vocabulary or normalizing the s forms.
The gloss specifies murmuring or disparaging others. Fitono begins an example concerning another person's name or reputation.
Nauo iycutaſu completes the act of speaking someone's name down, that is, damaging their reputation. Me- begins the Portuguese phrase menos cabo below.
Completes menos cabo da honra dalguem, detriment to someone's honour. The printed two-word menos cabo is retained rather than combined editorially.
Iydaxi means beginning to say or bringing something out in speech. The printed aita principal part is historical and is not modernized to dashita.
Iye means house or household; Iyeuo voſamuru illustrates governing a household. The initial is capital I, not the OCR long s.
Nar completes gouernar, governing the house. A second example, Iyeuo tatçuru, means building a house and begins its translation with Edifi-.
Car caſa completes edificar casa, building a house. This short physical line belongs to the second Iye example.
The separate verbal entry Iye, iyuru, iyeta means a wound, abscess, or illness healing. It is intransitive in contrast to the earlier iyaſu entry.
Qizuga iyeta means the wound healed, with ga marking the wound as subject. This confirms the intransitive sense rather than curing someone else.

runs.text: Tributo, ou finta que paga cada caſa.

lines.note: Iyebet denotes the tribute or assessment paid by each house. The final t is preserved as the printed checked-coda spelling, not expanded to a modern syllable.
Iyedomo first receives the adversative gloss but or however. A second explanation begins Dizendo across the physical line break.
Completes the verbal explanation and equates it with Mǒxedomo, although one says or speaks. The explanatory i is upright apparatus before the Japanese synonym, not Portuguese body type.

runs.text: Em comum, ou como as outras caſas..

lines.note: Iyenami means in common with, or on the same basis as, other households. Enlargement shows the s of outras raised above the preceding a, missed by OCR. Two terminal stop-like marks are retained; the second could instead be stray ink.
Iyenamino cuyacuuo tçutomuru describes fulfilling service obligations like the other households. The Portuguese translation begins Fazer at the line end.

runs.text: zer Cuyacu como as outras caſas.

lines.note: Completes the translation as performing Cuyacu like the other houses. Cuyacu is a Japanese service term embedded in the Portuguese sentence and is printed in its italic context.
Iyeno co is glossed here as a distant relative of a great lord, rather than simply a child of the household. The damaged Portuguese noun supports ſenhor, not OCR ſenhar; grã continues below.
De completes grande. Yacata exemplifies the lordly rank or household in the Portuguese explanation; the entire name is italic in this impression, not a lone roman Y followed by italic letters.
Iyezzuto is equated with Miague, a brought-back gift. The Portuguese begins a definition of the present rather than providing another Japanese expression.
Algũa couſa completes the printed definition of the gift. Couſa is retained as visible rather than replaced by a more expected word for a place.
Iyfagure describes being embarrassed through missing one's opportunity to speak. The initial capital I, partly weak, is recoverable before yfagure and was omitted by OCR.

runs.text: não falar, ou ſair a ſeu tempo.

lines.note: The embarrassment results from not speaking or not coming in at the right moment. This completes the timing-related sense of Iyfagure.
Iyfanaxi means speaking decisively or categorically. The example introduced by italic Vt follows on the next row.
Iyato iyfanaita means saying a firm no. The past ending -aita agrees with the printed principal parts and should not be modernized to -ashita.
Iyfaruqe means making something clear in words. The alternative dar razão begins an explanatory or justificatory sense.
Ayamariuo iyfaruquru illustrates explaining or accounting for a fault. The following Portuguese makes the defensive sense explicit.

runs.text: Eſcuſarſe, ou dar razão da falta, ou crime q̃

lines.note: The translation is excusing oneself or giving an account of an alleged fault or crime. The abbreviated q̃ remains unexpanded in the transcription.
Lhe impoem completes the allegation: a fault or crime imputed to the person. This short row is integral to the defence example.
Iyfataracaxi corresponds to speaking effectively or eloquently. The scan supports t in fataracaxi, matching the hatarakasu-based form, rather than OCR Iyfafaracaxi.
Quentemente completes eloquentemente, explaining the quality of effective speech. It is not a new entry or a displaced caption.

runs.text: Dar rezão de ſi, ou de ou-

lines.note: Iyfiraqi means explaining or defending oneself, with a further alternative continued on the next page. The scan supports initial I and Portuguese rezão; the printed ou- matches the following tra continuation.
The visible signature reads M n 2. The second letter is damaged and may represent an intended m, but the surviving two-stem n-like form is retained rather than regularized.
